title: Mean confused with median
description: The learner reports the median when the mean is asked, or vice versa.

title: Sum reported instead of mean
description: The learner adds the values but forgets to divide by the count.

title: Decimal given instead of percentage
description: The learner gives the proportion where the percentage was asked for, answering 0.3 when 30% was wanted. The two are the same quantity in different clothes, and the question's wording is the only thing that distinguishes them.

title: Percentage given instead of decimal
description: The learner gives the percentage figure where the proportion was asked for, answering 30 when 0.3 was wanted. Both describe the same share, so the number is not wrong so much as wearing the wrong form for what the question asked.

title: Fraction reversed
description: The learner writes the two numbers in the order the question mentioned them rather than the order the fraction needs, so "3 of the 4 boats" becomes 4/3. The quantities are both right and only their roles are exchanged, which is why the answer looks reasonable to the learner who wrote it.

title: Mean treated as outlier-resistant
description: The learner treats the mean as a fixed description of the group and expects one unusual value to leave it alone. Every value entering the sum is exactly why it does not, but a summary that is meant to stand for a whole set does feel as though it should be steady.

title: Chart axis misread
description: The learner compares the bars or points without first checking what each axis measures, and answers about the wrong quantity or the wrong case. A chart invites you to look before you read, and the picture is legible enough that the labels feel optional.

title: Correlation read as causation
description: The learner sees two quantities rising together and concludes that one drives the other. Reading a pattern as an explanation is what patterns are for most of the time, so this is the ordinary habit misapplied rather than a lapse in care — and nothing in the data itself rules the conclusion out.

title: Coordinate axes swapped
description: The learner plots (y, x) instead of (x, y) — the right pair of numbers, applied to the wrong axes.

title: Digits treated as numerical data
description: A variable written with digits (boat number, postcode) is classified as numerical even though its values are labels, not quantities.

title: The count changes between passes
description: The learner accepts two different totals for the same collection, treating a skipped or double-counted item as a property of the counting direction rather than an error.

title: The carried ten is dropped
description: When a column adds to more than nine the learner writes the units digit and forgets to carry the ten into the next column.

title: Digits subtracted in whichever order avoids borrowing
description: Within a column the learner takes the smaller digit from the larger one regardless of which is on top, instead of borrowing.

title: Multiplying treated as adding
description: The learner adds the two numbers instead of counting equal groups, so 7 x 4 is answered as 11.

title: Divided the wrong way round
description: The learner divides the number of groups by the amount being shared instead of the other way round.

title: Bigger bottom number read as a bigger fraction
description: The learner compares fractions by the size of the denominator alone, so 1/8 is judged larger than 1/4 because 8 is larger than 4.

title: More digits read as a bigger decimal
description: The learner compares decimals by how many digits follow the point, treating 0.25 as larger than 0.5 because it is longer.

title: A ratio part treated as a share of the whole
description: Given a ratio of 3 parts to 5 parts, the learner reports the first part as 3/5 of the mixture instead of 3/8.

title: Scaling by adding instead of multiplying
description: The learner keeps a difference constant rather than a ratio, so if 2 crates cost 6 coins they conclude 4 crates cost 8 coins.

title: Negatives ordered by their digits
description: The learner compares negative numbers by the digit after the minus sign, so -12 is judged larger than -7 because 12 is larger than 7.

title: Ticks counted instead of the scale being read
description: On a line whose labelled marks are more than one unit apart, the learner counts marks as if each were worth one, landing at a fraction of the intended value.

title: Right row, wrong column
description: The learner locates the correct case in a table but reads the value from a neighbouring column, answering a different variable's value.

title: A constant column counted as a variable
description: A column holding the same value on every row is treated as a variable simply because it has a header.

title: Cases and observations confused
description: Asked how many cases a dataset holds, the learner answers the number of recorded values — rows times columns — instead of the number of rows.

title: Categories counted instead of cases
description: Asked for the frequency of one category, the learner reports how many different categories the variable has.

title: The first repeat taken as the only mode
description: The learner stops at the first value seen to repeat and reports it as the mode, missing a second value that repeats as often or more.

title: Skew named after the bulk rather than the tail
description: The learner names the direction of skew from the side holding most of the data, so a set with a long high tail and a crowd of small values is called left-skewed. The reasoning is consistent and the answer is the exact opposite of the convention.

title: The range reported as the largest value
description: The learner reads 'how far the data reaches' as 'how high it goes' and reports the maximum instead of the difference between the two ends. The answer is a real reading from the set, which is what makes it hard to spot.

title: A quartile's position reported instead of its value
description: The learner works out correctly how far along the sorted row the cut falls and then reports that position as the answer, rather than reading off the value sitting there. The arithmetic is right and the answer is an index rather than a measurement.

title: A percentile counted from the wrong side
description: The learner counts the readings above the mark instead of those at or below it, and reports that share as the percentile. The arithmetic is sound and the answer is the complement of the right one, so it looks entirely plausible on a value near the middle.

title: The interquartile range computed from the extremes
description: The learner subtracts the smallest reading from the largest — the range — while calling it the interquartile range. The two are the same shape of calculation on different pairs of numbers, which is what makes the substitution easy to miss.

title: Spread measured by averaging raw distances
description: The learner averages the distances from the mean without squaring them, and reports the result as a measure of spread. The arithmetic is correct and the answer is zero for every dataset, which is what makes it a misconception about what the mean is rather than a slip.

title: The variance reported where the standard deviation was asked for
description: The learner computes the variance correctly and stops there, reporting a figure in squared units as though it were a distance. The number is right for a different question, and the units are the only thing that gives it away.

title: The gaps between bars read as missing data
description: The learner takes the space between two bars to mean something absent — a day with no catch, a category nobody recorded — rather than the separation between two named groups. The reading is a reasonable one for a picture with a continuous axis, and wrong for a categorical one.

title: A histogram bar read as a single value
description: The learner reads a histogram as though it were a bar chart, taking each bar to report the count of one exact reading rather than of every reading in an interval. The number is read off correctly and attached to the wrong thing.

title: A box plot's widths read as quantities
description: The learner reads a long whisker or a wide box as holding more readings than a short one, rather than the same quarter spread over more ground. The reading is natural for anyone arriving from bar charts and histograms, where width or height does mean amount.

title: A dot plot's stack height read as the value
description: The learner reads how many dots are in the tallest column and reports that count as the mode, rather than the value the column stands over. Both numbers are on the picture and only one answers the question.

title: A scatterplot point read as a single measurement
description: The learner reads a point's position on one axis and treats it as the whole reading, or counts points as though the height of a region were a total. Every earlier chart in the curriculum encodes one variable, so carrying that habit across is the natural error.

title: Bar heights read as amounts on a truncated axis
description: The learner compares bar lengths without checking where the value axis starts, and reads a sixfold difference in height as a sixfold difference in the data. The reading is the one a bar chart normally invites, which is precisely what a truncated axis exploits.

title: Equal centres read as equal datasets
description: The learner sees two datasets sharing a mean or a median and concludes they behave alike. The centre is the summary a report leads with, so treating it as the comparison is the natural error rather than a careless one — and it is exactly what a shared median cannot support.
